# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) has transformed the prevention of sudden cardiac death in patients at risk for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [1]. However, the transvenous ICD (TV-ICD) carries well-documented risks related to the intravascular leads, including lead failure, venous occlusion, tricuspid valve injury, and systemic infection requiring complex lead extraction [2,3]. The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to circumvent these lead-related complications by avoiding intravascular and intracardiac placement entirely [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, evidence base, clinical outcomes, and limitations of the S-ICD.

## Device Design and Rationale

The S-ICD consists of a pulse generator implanted in the left lateral thoracic region and a subcutaneous parasternal lead with sensing electrodes [4,5]. The entire system lies outside the thoracic cavity and great vessels, eliminating the risks of lead-related vascular and cardiac injury [5]. Early feasibility work established that an entirely subcutaneous configuration could reliably detect ventricular fibrillation and deliver a defibrillation shock, typically at 80 J [4]. Because the system lacks transvenous leads, it cannot provide long-term antitachycardia or bradycardia pacing, although it does deliver transient post-shock pacing [6].

## Clinical Evidence

The pivotal IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry provided foundational safety and efficacy data, demonstrating high rates of successful conversion of induced ventricular fibrillation and acceptable complication profiles [7,8]. Pooled analyses of these cohorts confirmed durable performance, with conversion efficacy exceeding 98% and low rates of device-related infection requiring extraction [9,10]. Subsequent registries reinforced the relative ease of system removal compared with transvenous lead extraction [11].

The landmark PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomized comparison of the S-ICD with the TV-ICD in patients with an indication for defibrillation but no need for pacing [12]. The S-ICD was noninferior to the TV-ICD for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [12]. Notably, lead-related complications were less frequent with the S-ICD, while inappropriate shocks—predominantly due to T-wave oversensing—were a recurring concern [12,13]. The UNTOUCHED study specifically evaluated inappropriate shock rates using contemporary programming and demonstrated markedly reduced inappropriate therapy when high-rate detection zones and SMART Pass filtering were employed [14,15].

## Patient Selection and Screening

Appropriate candidate selection is critical because sensing relies on surface-like vector analysis [16]. Preimplant electrocardiographic screening, using either manual templates or automated screening tools, identifies patients whose QRS-T morphology is suitable in multiple body positions [16,17]. Failure of screening, often related to tall T waves or high R-wave amplitude variation, predicts oversensing and is more common in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and certain channelopathies [17,18]. The S-ICD is particularly attractive for young patients, those with prior device infections, patients with limited venous access, and individuals on hemodialysis at high infectious risk [19,20]. Guidelines endorse the S-ICD as an alternative to the TV-ICD when pacing for bradycardia, cardiac resynchronization, or antitachycardia therapy is not required [21,22].

## Implantation Technique and Outcomes

Refinements in implantation, including the two-incision technique and intermuscular generator placement, have improved cosmetic outcomes and reduced complications [23,24]. Defibrillation testing at implantation has traditionally been performed to confirm adequate shock vectors, although its routine necessity is increasingly debated [25]. The PRAETORIAN-DFT study evaluated chest radiography-based assessment of device position as an alternative to conventional defibrillation testing [26].

## Limitations and Complications

The principal limitations of the S-ICD remain the absence of bradycardia and antitachycardia pacing and a larger generator with higher energy requirements [6,27]. Inappropriate shocks, infection, and erosion are the most frequently reported adverse events [13,27]. Longer-term battery longevity and the inability to terminate monomorphic ventricular tachycardia painlessly are relevant considerations in patients with structural heart disease and slow, well-tolerated tachycardias [27,28].

## Future Directions

The integration of the S-ICD with the leadless pacemaker represents a major advance, enabling modular communication to provide antitachycardia and antibradycardia pacing without transvenous leads [29]. The MODULAR ATP study demonstrated the feasibility and safety of such combined leadless systems, potentially addressing the chief limitation of the S-ICD [29]. Continued improvements in sensing algorithms, generator size, and battery technology are expected to broaden eligibility [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD provides effective protection against sudden cardiac death while avoiding the vascular and lead-related complications of transvenous systems [12]. Randomized and registry data support its noninferiority for appropriately selected patients who do not require pacing [12,14]. With evolving leadless pacing integration, the S-ICD is poised to play an expanding role in arrhythmia management [29].
